source.heading: The passage

docMeta.dd: The Cheshire Cat, to Alice — both fictional characters

source.excerpt:
“In that direction,” the Cat said, waving its right paw round, “lives a Hatter: and in that direction,” waving the other paw, “lives a March Hare. Visit either you like: they’re both mad.”

“But I don’t want to go among mad people,” Alice remarked.

“Oh, you can’t help that,” said the Cat: “we’re all mad here. I’m mad. You’re mad.”

“How do you know I’m mad?” said Alice.

“You must be,” said the Cat, “or you wouldn’t have come here.”
trail: Checked against the full text, not a quotation site. The passage appears verbatim in the complete Project Gutenberg edition of Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland ↗, in Chapter VI, “Pig and Pepper” — the chapter that ends with Alice walking off toward the March Hare’s house.

Independently confirmed on Wikiquote. The Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland page ↗ transcribes the same exchange, in the same chapter, with the same wording, and marks it as one of the book’s best-known passages.

The 1866 first edition is on Wikisource. The Wikisource text of Chapter VI in the 1866 Macmillan edition ↗ carries the book as originally issued, for anyone who wants to check the wording against the earliest widely circulated printing rather than a modern transcription.
source.excerptNote: The popular quotation usually stops at “You’re mad” — which loses the Cat’s actual argument. His proof that Alice is mad is that she turned up at all.

source.rightsNote: Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland was first published by Macmillan in November 1865 and Carroll died in 1898, so the text is long out of copyright in the United States and free to reproduce. Note that this applies to Carroll’s words: John Tenniel’s original illustrations are likewise public domain, but a particular modern edition’s typesetting, notes or new artwork may not be.

author.heading: About Lewis Carroll
author.bio: Lewis Carroll was the pen name of Charles Lutwidge Dodgson, a mathematics lecturer at Christ Church, Oxford. Under the pseudonym he wrote Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland (1865) and Through the Looking-Glass (1871); under his own name he published on geometry and logic. He was also a prolific letter-writer, and a good deal of what circulates as “Carroll” online comes from that correspondence rather than the Alice books.

misattribution.heading: What usually goes wrong
misattribution.intro: Nobody disputes that Carroll wrote this. What travels badly is who says it and where it stops.

items.why: The line is routinely captioned as the Hatter’s, helped by a century of illustration and film. It is the Cheshire Cat’s, and the Hatter has not appeared yet — the Cat is in the middle of giving Alice directions to him.

Most reproductions end at “I’m mad. You’re mad.” The exchange continues for two more lines, and the Cat’s reasoning — “You must be, or you wouldn’t have come here” — is the part that makes it a joke rather than a slogan.

misattribution.truthLine: Carroll wrote it, the Cheshire Cat says it, and it sits in Chapter VI of Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland ↗.

context.heading: Why the Cat gets the good line
lead: The Cheshire Cat is the only creature in Wonderland who knows he is in Wonderland. Everyone else is busy being absurd; the Cat is the one commenting on the absurdity, which is why Carroll gives him the book’s tidiest piece of logic and its most quotable shrug.

The exchange also does real work in the plot: it is the Cat’s directions that send Alice to the March Hare, and so into the tea-party in the following chapter. The line people quote as free-floating philosophy is, in the book, a set of walking directions with an argument attached.
context.pull: The only creature in Wonderland who knows he is in Wonderland.
